rv.q: Small, significant gestures add poignant realism to even the show’s strangest, silliest moments.
However, the content-light third act loses pace and exposes some fairly blunt messaging.
It’s an imaginative, often engrossing ride.
Nevertheless, the notion of loss and death gives the piece its much needed shadows.
Aside from the underdone setting, Hope has a Happy Meal manages to be both funny and exciting, with well-written and enjoyably performed characters and confident, clear direction.
The production sparks with peppery wit, partly thanks to its unapologetically sui generis sense of surreal black humour.
Despite the details of the post-democratic corporate country being too light, it’s still pleasing.
Unfortunately, however, Fowler’s play is both incoherent and thin – despite its ambitions to apply a Swiftian satire to many pressing problems of the modern age.
So welcome another play that offers a great summer of surreal new writing.
Fowler’s settling into himself; definitely both worth seeing and pursuing.
It’s a little bit all these things, which makes it an entertaining play but not overly provocative.
A Happy Meal fails at both, with not much to take away.
Hope has a Happy Meal is a gripping triumph of new writing.

cn.t: Critics find this dystopian satire visually striking and well-performed, with strong comedic moments, but fault the script for losing focus as family drama overtakes its hyper-capitalist critique.
